extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians conducting inter-rater/intra-rater reliability studies (healthcare, rehabilitation, diagnostic testing, measurement)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, statistics, and reporting practices for measuring, interpreting, and improving inter-rater and intra-rater reliability (kappa, ICC, percent agreement, etc.) across clinical and research measurement instruments. Covers choice of statistic by data type, adjustments (prevalence/bias), training effects, and reporting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen's kappa (kappa statistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The kappa statistic is frequently used to test interrater reliability; it was introduced by Jacob Cohen in 1960 to account for chance agreement. Like most correlation statistics, the kappa can range from -1 to +1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for categorical data to account for chance agreement. Note limitations: affected by prevalence and bias; interpretation thresholds (e.g., Cohen's suggested interpretation) may be too lenient for health research (e.g., 0.41 might be considered acceptable by Cohen but questioned in healthcare). Report kappa with 95% confidence intervals and consider its assumptions (independent subjects and independent raters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Percent agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Percent agreement is calculated as the number of agreement scores divided by the total number of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percent agreement alongside kappa because percent agreement is intuitive but does not account for chance agreement; can be useful to contextualize kappa, especially when kappa is low despite high percent agreement. Break down into positive/negative agreement when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted kappa (for ordinal data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weighted kappa assigns weights to disagreements and is used for ordinal (graded) categorical data; with weighting, kappa values are often higher than unweighted kappa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weighted kappa when categories are ordered (e.g., rating scales). Specify the weighting scheme (linear/quadratic). Consider comparing weighted vs unweighted kappa and report both if informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fleiss' multirater kappa (and other multirater kappas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fleiss multirater kappa is used to estimate agreement among >2 raters for categorical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate multirater kappa when more than two raters are involved. Report proportion agreement and multirater kappa, and indicate handling of ties and missing ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)
rubrics_metrics.description: ICC is used to measure reliability for continuous or Likert-scale data; different ICC models (e.g., ICC2,1; ICC3,1) and forms (single-measure, average-measure) are used depending on study design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and report the ICC model that matches your design (e.g., random vs fixed raters, single vs average measures). Report ICC with 95% confidence intervals. Use ICC for perceptual/Likert items and continuous measurements; complement with Bland–Altman analyses for agreement where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion agreement and Fleiss/Kappa complements (positive/negative agreement, prevalence index, bias index)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary agreement measures such as positive/negative agreement, prevalence index, and bias index quantify different facets of agreement and help interpret kappa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate and report these supplemental indices to interpret kappa's sensitivity to prevalence and bias. Use them to explain paradoxes (e.g., high percent agreement but low kappa due to skewed prevalence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK)
rubrics_metrics.description: PABAK adjusts kappa for effects of prevalence and bias, often increasing apparent agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report PABAK when prevalence or bias distort standard kappa. Compare PABAK to Cohen's kappa to show the effect of prevalence/bias adjustments and caution in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: AC1 / Gwet's agreement coefficient
rubrics_metrics.description: AC1 (sometimes reported as Gwet's AC1) is an alternative agreement statistic less affected by prevalence and bias than kappa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider AC1 when kappa is problematic due to prevalence; report alongside kappa to provide a robustness check. Provide confidence intervals and interpretation thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomization / collapsing categories to improve reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplifying multi-category scales into dichotomous outcomes (or collapsing categories) can increase percent agreement and kappa values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dichotomization only when clinically or conceptually justifiable; report both original and collapsed analyses, because simplification can mask important distinctions and affect validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bland–Altman analysis, SEM and MDC (agreement for continuous measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bland–Altman plots and measures like the standard error of measurement (SEM) and minimal detectable change (MDC95) assess agreement and absolute measurement error for continuous outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Bland–Altman for continuous data to visualize bias and limits of agreement. Report SEM and MDC95 to quantify absolute measurement error and clinical relevance. Complement ICC (relative reliability) with Bland–Altman (absolute agreement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test–retest, intra-rater and inter-rater reliability distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability studies should distinguish and measure inter-rater (between raters), intra-rater (within same rater over time), and test–retest reliability (stability over repeated administrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies to capture the appropriate form(s) of reliability for your instrument. Report each type separately with appropriate statistics (e.g., Cohen's kappa for intra-rater categorical repeat, ICC for intra-rater continuous repeat). Consider timing, blinding, and whether treatment/intervention occurs between measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate statistic by data type and rater count
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the reliability statistic based on data scale (nominal/ordinal/interval) and number of raters (2 vs >2): Cohen's kappa for two raters categorical, weighted kappa for ordinal, Fleiss or other multirater kappas for >2 raters, ICC for continuous/Likert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly justify the chosen statistic in the methods. If multiple data types exist in the instrument, report different statistics per item and for composite scores. For composite/averaged scores prefer ICC and report kappa for categorical classification decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions required for correct use of kappa
rubrics_metrics.description: Kappa requires data measured on a categorical scale, independent patients/objects, and independent measurement decisions by observers/raters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure study design meets these assumptions or state and justify deviations. Violations (e.g., non-independence of observations or raters influencing each other) invalidate kappa and require alternative approaches or adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and power considerations for kappa/ICC
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability statistics have sample size and power requirements; small samples can lead to wide confidence intervals and unstable kappa/ICC estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sample size to achieve acceptable precision for kappa/ICC estimates (reported CIs). State power/sample-size rationale in methods. Be cautious interpreting kappa values from small N or few events/categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report confidence intervals and statistical uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability coefficients should be reported with 95% confidence intervals (and p-values where relevant) to show precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always provide CIs for kappa, ICC, AC1, etc., and discuss practical/clinical significance, not just statistical significance. When reporting ranges across items/rater pairs, present medians/interquartile ranges as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of GRRAS and reporting guidelines for reliability studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting in some studies is in accordance with proposed guidelines for the reporting of reliability and agreement studies (GRRAS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow GRRAS (or similar) for complete transparent reporting: describe raters, training, blinding, sample selection, timing between ratings, statistics used, and provide CIs and interpretation. Use standardized reporting to aid meta-analysis and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rater training and anchoring to improve reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Focused, video-based anchor training and achieving pre-data-collection agreement (e.g., ≥80%) can improve inter-rater reliability, especially among less-experienced raters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include systematic training (examples, anchor videos, written instructions) and, if possible, require raters to reach a predefined agreement threshold before data collection. Report training content and effect (pre/post reliability comparisons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rater experience and context on reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rater experience, familiarity with instruments, and contextual factors (urban/rural setting, case mix, prevalence) influence reliability estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and report subgroup reliability by rater experience and setting. Discuss how variability in case prevalence and clarity of operational definitions affects agreement and may require refined categories or improved definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity measures alongside reliability (sensitivity, specificity, AUC, construct validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing a triage system or tool's validity (e.g., sensitivity, specificity, AUC, construct validity) is necessary in addition to reliability metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the instrument is used for decision-making (e.g., triage), report validity metrics (sensitivity/specificity/AUC) together with reliability; a tool can be reliable but not valid. For construct validity, compare classifications against reference standards and report kappa or other agreement with original classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of measurement instrument and item-level reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Some instruments or individual items may show poor reliability (e.g., sensory perception, nutrition items); item-level reliability analysis can identify weak components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both total/composite scores and individual item reliabilities. Consider removing, redefining, or re-training on items with low item-level reliability. Report which items have unacceptable reliability and discuss implications for the instrument's use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative agreement statistics (Kendall's tau-B for validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other statistics such as Kendall's tau-B may be used for validity calculations or ordinal associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select alternative association/validity statistics when data characteristics warrant (e.g., ordinal validity comparisons). Report choice and interpret in context of other reliability metrics.
